explanations.explanation: This neuron isn’t tracking meaning or part-of-speech at all but rather a handful of mid-word BPE substrings—chiefly those built around “e” (ew, lem, ost, as, etc.). In other words, it’s an orthographic n-gram detector that spikes on certain “e”-containing subword chunks regardless of their semantic context.

This neuron isn’t about any particular topic or language – it simply lights up on BPE subword fragments, especially the little “morpheme-like” roots and affixes you see in English (and occasionally other languages): things like onom- in “astronomical,” cept- in “conception,” pet- in “competitor,” lig- in “eligibility,” etc. It’s effectively a detector for those mid-word letter sequences (common Greek/Latin roots and suffixes).

This neuron fires on the very first word of a document‐style header or metadata line (the “front‐matter” of articles or section titles), flagging tokens like “Originally,” “American,” “Olympic,” “America’s,” “Michelle,” or “Fifteen” whenever they kick off a heading or provenance line.

This neuron detects consonant‐heavy subword fragments (e.g. “idd,” “uvik,” “utt,” “rb,” “ibr,” “arr,” “ond”) that most often occur in the middle of proper names, brands, products or other specialized terms.
This feature fires on garbled or non-standard Unicode artifacts (e.g. the “�” replacement character and similar odd symbols), effectively flagging encoding/formatting anomalies in the text.

This feature marks the first, discourse-shifting word of a new sentence or list-item heading—those big, capitalized openers (What, When, Over, There, Despite, etc.) that signal a fresh section, question or bullet in a document.
This feature is a detector for in‐text personal names—especially English given names (e.g. Susannah, Colleen, Caitlyn, Naomi, Laura, Agatha, etc.)—marking proper‐noun tokens that name individuals.

The activation patterns across all four groups show that this neuron is not picking up meaning so much as orthographic shape: it fires whenever the subword token begins with a specific two‐ or three‐letter uppercase prefix.  Concretely:  
• Feature “Sw” → any token whose first two letters are “Sw” (Swannanoa, Swanton, Swanswell, Swimmers, Swim, …)  
• Feature “Gen” → any token starting “Gen” (Genuine, Genius, Genesis, Genomic, …)  
• Feature “Spe” → any token starting “Spe” (Speaker, Speech, Special, …)  
• Feature “Sn” → any token starting “Sn” (Snap, Snafu, Snugabell, …)

This neuron lights up on the “front-matter” of a post or reply—the little discourse markers and headings that kick off a message (greetings like “hi everyone,” polite openers like “thanks” or “well,” topic-introduction words like “cost,” “list,” “what,” numbered headings, etc.). It flags the tokens that serve to launch or frame a new post or turn.

This feature lights up on attributive past-participial adjectives (the “-ed” form) that describe a prepared, processed or conditioned state—especially in marketing or product-listing contexts (e.g. “baked goods,” “printed music,” “flooded basements,” “whipped cream,” “augmented reality”).

This feature fires whenever the model is looking at a BPE “continuation” subtoken – i.e. a piece of a longer word rather than a standalone token. You can see it spiking on fragments like “and” in Demand, “it” in Merit, “ple” in Compleat, “imal” in primal, “st” in first, “ro” in Afro, “ud” in Muddy, “lem” in Flemish, “ong” in Hong, “ut” in Bruton, etc.

This feature lights up on the very first, standalone “heading” word of a prompt or section—typically an imperative (Register, Fill) or an introductory preposition (From) used as a call-to-action or section title in forms and promotional/instructional copy.

This neuron fires on the “In + NOUN” scaffolding of English adverbial clauses—e.g. “in order to,” “in case,” “in need of,” “in accordance with”—that introduce purpose, condition, necessity or conformity.

This neuron lights up on sentence‐ or list-level “cue” words and short phrases—things like see, right, interesting, take, then, complete, combine, etc.—that serve as discourse or instruction markers introducing new points, steps, or emphasis.
This feature is a toponym detector that fires on the “Cod” element of the place name “Cape Cod,” marking references to that New England locale.

This neuron is simply a “ret”-substring detector – it lights up whenever the token “ret” (as in “accretionary” and its kin) appears, so it ends up marking words built on the Latin “-cretion/-cretionary” root and thus correlates with geological‐accretion contexts.

1) “obby” – the character sequence “obby,” as in “Lobby,” identifying room or common‐area names in institutional or campus contexts.  
2) “BP” – the uppercase bigram “BP,” marking a brand or product‐line prefix (e.g. “BPWORLD”) in furniture or industrial descriptions.  
3) “ody” – the suffix “ody,” which surfaces in biological terms such as “antibody.”  
4) “ilon” – the substring “ilon,” found in cosmetic or skincare product names (e.g. “Sensitive‐Creme”).  
5) “tochrome” – the fragment of “cytochrome,” flagging biochemical compound names.  
6) “Cedar” – the proper‐noun “Cedar,” used in place or company names (parks, textiles, catering, realty).  
7) “iod” – the stem “iod,” as in “biodiversity,” highlighting biological‐diversity terminology.  
8) “inos” – the substring “inos,” found in “inositol” within biochemical or medical contexts.  
9) “RP” – the uppercase bigram “RP,” used as a product‐code prefix in mechanical/piston‐ring part listings.  
10) “rost” – the fragment “rost,” appearing in “Frosted,” flagging bakery or event names.  
11) “Austin” – the given name “Austin,” marking personnel announcements in corporate bios.  
12) “rut” – the substring “rut,” found in “ruthenium” during chemical assay descriptions.  
13) “ryan” – the sequence “ryan,” as in “Bryan/Ryan,” indicating personal names in interviews and academic profiles.  
14) “carbon” – the full word “carbon,” highlighting references to activated‐carbon materials or catalysts.

This feature detects bibliographic‐reference structures and the act of referring—e.g. author/editor lists, titles, years, journals or proceedings, “In …,” “Abstract,” “paper,” “reprinted,” “refer(ring) to,” etc.—marking when the text is citing or pointing to a publication.

This neuron fires on domain- or category-label nouns—especially formal or regulatory sectors, agencies and topic keywords (e.g. Tobacco, dependency, oil, gas, capital gains, Food, Water, Occupational, Litigation)—i.e. it flags words that name a specialized domain or organizational area.

This neuron fires whenever the model is naming up a countable entity or “thing” – whether it’s a piece of furniture (desk, chair, cupboard), a food unit (eggs), a sports stat (rebounds, tackles), a vehicle/haul operator (haulers), a location or object (garage, warehouse, Francisco), even time‐unit nouns (quarter). In short, it marks the mention of concrete, countable nouns.
